kernels.definition: A variable is a name that refers to a stored value; the assignment operator = binds the name on the left to the value produced on the right (for objects it binds the reference, so no copy is made).

definitionAnchor.quote: Variables allow programs to refer to values using names rather than memory locations

facts.text: A statement sets a variable to a value using the assignment operator (=), with the name on the left and the value on the right.

anchor.quote: A statement can set a variable to a value using the assignment operator (=)

facts.text: Assignment is not mathematical equality — = copies a value into a variable rather than asserting two sides are equal.

anchor.quote: Note that this is different from the equal sign of mathematics

facts.text: A variable name may contain letters, digits, and underscores and be any length, but cannot start with a digit.

anchor.quote: A variable name can consist of letters, digits, and underscores and be of any length

facts.text: Variable names are case-sensitive, so total and Total are two different variables.

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §1.3 Variables

kernels.definition: Every Python value has a data type (such as int, float, or str); expressions combine values, and conversion functions move a value from one type to another.

definitionAnchor.quote: explicit type conversion to convert one data type to another

facts.text: The interpreter performs implicit type conversion to promote types automatically inside a mixed expression.

anchor.quote: The Python interpreter uses implicit type conversion to automatically convert one data type to another

facts.text: int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3.

anchor.quote: int() converts a data type to an integer. Any fractional part is removed

facts.text: True division (/) converts numbers to floats before dividing and always returns a float.

anchor.quote: True division (/) converts numbers to floats before dividing

facts.text: Floor division (//) computes the whole-number quotient, discarding the remainder.

anchor.quote: Floor division (//) computes the quotient, or the number of times divided

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §2.2 Type conversion; §2.5 Dividing integers

kernels.definition: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.

definitionAnchor.quote: When an if-else statement is executed, one and only one of the branches is taken

facts.text: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.

anchor.quote: If the condition is true, the body is executed. If the condition is false, the body is not executed

facts.text: An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.

anchor.quote: An else statement is used with an if statement and contains a body of statements that is executed when the if statement's condition is false

facts.text: and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.

anchor.quote: The and operator takes two condition operands and returns True if both conditions are true

attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §4.2 If-else statements; §4.3 Boolean operations

mcItems.q: In the line count = count + 1, what does the assignment operator do?
op: Checks whether both sides are equal
Binds count to the value produced on the right
Creates two variables with the same name
Deletes the old value stored in count
mcItems.ex: B is correct because assignment places the result of the right-hand expression into the name on the left. A is the common misconception: = in Python assignment is not a test for equality.

mcItems.q: Which variable name is valid in Python?
mcItems.ex: B is correct because variable names may include letters, digits, and underscores, and they cannot start with a digit. A is the common mistake: it starts with a digit. The other choices use an invalid hyphen or a space.

keyTerms.df: A statement that gives a name a value by putting the name on the left of = and the value on the right.
keyTerms.eg: x = 5 stores 5 in x in a short tracing exercise.
keyTerms.mi: It means the same thing as mathematical equality.
keyTerms.cx: In Python, = is used to set a variable, not to test whether two expressions are equal.

keyTerms.df: Names that are treated as different when their letters use different capitalization.
keyTerms.eg: total and Total can refer to two different variables in a trace of a program.
keyTerms.mi: Changing only capitalization leaves the name unchanged.
keyTerms.cx: Python distinguishes total from Total, so the capitalization matters.

mcItems.q: A student types `int(3.9)` while tracing a program. What value should they expect, and why?
op: 3, because the number is rounded up
3, because the fractional part is removed
4, because Python always rounds to the nearest whole number
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is 3, because `int()` drops the fractional part instead of rounding. A common misconception is to expect rounding to the nearest whole number, but `int(3.9)` truncates to 3.

mcItems.q: A program evaluates `7 / 2` and `7 // 2`. Which pair of results matches Python’s rules?
mcItems.ex: `/` performs true division and returns a float, so `7 / 2` is 3.5. `//` performs floor division and gives the whole-number quotient, so `7 // 2` is 3. A likely misconception is to swap these operations or treat `//` as ordinary decimal division.

keyTerms.df: A change that turns a value from one data type into another.
keyTerms.eg: A trace of `int(3.9)` shows a float becoming an integer before the program keeps going.
keyTerms.mi: It only happens when the programmer writes an explicit conversion function.
keyTerms.cx: Python can also promote types automatically inside a mixed expression, and `int()` is one explicit way to convert.

keyTerms.df: An integer-style quotient that drops any remainder.
keyTerms.eg: In `7 // 2`, the result is `3`, which is the whole-number quotient.
keyTerms.mi: It means dividing and then rounding to the nearest whole number.
keyTerms.cx: The operation discards the remainder rather than rounding; the related decimal-producing operator is `/`.

mcItems.q: In a short Python program, you want to print a reminder only when the user enters a value greater than 10. Which control-flow structure fits best?
mcItems.ex: A plain if statement fits because it runs its body only when the condition is true. The common misconception is to pick a loop or exception handler for every decision, but those structures solve different problems.

mcItems.q: A program should show one message when a test score is passing and a different message when it is not. Which structure matches that behavior?
mcItems.ex: An if-else statement matches because it chooses exactly one branch: the if body when the condition is true, or the else body when it is false. A likely misconception is that a single if can cover both outcomes, but it skips its body when the condition is false.

keyTerms.df: A control structure that selects a code path according to whether a condition evaluates to true or false.
keyTerms.eg: If a temperature is below freezing, print a warning; otherwise, continue normally.
keyTerms.mi: It always runs both branches.
keyTerms.cx: Only one branch runs, and an if-else chooses exactly one branch based on the condition.

keyTerms.df: A logic word used to combine or modify conditions.
keyTerms.eg: Use and to require two tests, or to accept either one, and not to flip a test.
keyTerms.mi: These operators are only for comparing numbers.
keyTerms.cx: They build compound conditions: and is true only when both parts are true, or is true when either part is true, and not reverses one condition.
